title: Topic Drill: Reading Informational Texts (Set D)

items.stem:
Notice: The Redfern College Career Fair takes place Thursday in the gymnasium from ten until two. More than thirty employers, from hospitals to software firms, will staff tables. Students should bring several printed resumes and dress as they would for an interview. Short workshops on handshakes and self-introductions run in the library every hour. Admission is free, no registration is required, and light snacks will be offered in the lobby.

Which statement best expresses the main idea of the notice?
options: Students must register early to attend the workshops in the library.
Hospitals and software firms are competing for the same graduates.
Students are invited to a free event where they can meet employers.
The gymnasium will be closed for the entire week of the event.
items.explanation: The notice announces a free fair with many employers and gives practical tips, so inviting students to meet employers sums it up. Registration is said to be unnecessary, no competition between firms is described, and the gymnasium is used for the event, not closed. Those choices twist small details into the central point.

items.stem:
Four employers confirmed booths at the Redfern Career Fair by Monday. Each is hiring for the coming summer, and students may apply at the booth on the day.

Employer | Field | Hiring for
North Clinic | Healthcare | Summer aides
Brightline Apps | Software | Interns
Cedar Bank | Finance | Tellers
Harbor Parks | Recreation | Camp leaders

Which booth should a student visit who hopes to supervise children in a seasonal job?
options: Harbor Parks
North Clinic
Brightline Apps
Cedar Bank
items.explanation: Only Harbor Parks lists camp leaders, a role that involves supervising children during the summer. North Clinic hires aides for healthcare, Brightline Apps seeks software interns, and Cedar Bank needs tellers who handle money. Matching the job named in the last column to the student’s goal is the only reliable method.

items.stem:
Devika Olsen runs the employer desk at the career fair, and colleagues describe her as meticulous. She checks each table label twice, confirms that every outlet works, and keeps a binder listing which employer arrives at what time. Last year, when a banner was hung a few inches crooked, she noticed it before the doors opened and had it fixed.

As used in the passage, the word “meticulous” most nearly means?
options: easily upset by changes in plans
friendly toward people she has just met
quick to finish tasks without checking them
extremely careful about small details
items.explanation: Checking labels twice, testing outlets and spotting a crooked banner all show close attention to detail. Being upset by changes is not described, her friendliness is never mentioned, and speed is contradicted by the repeated double checking. The context supplies the definition, so rereading the examples works better than guessing from the sound of the word.

items.stem:
Dear Mr. Pruitt, thank you for talking with me at the fair. When I said I had never repaired a bicycle, you explained that your shop trains new hires for two weeks before they help customers. Since then I have watched three repair videos and borrowed my uncle’s tools to practice on an old frame. I would welcome the chance to interview for the weekend position.

Which inference about the writer is best supported by the letter?
options: The writer already has years of repair experience.
The writer is willing to take initiative to prepare for the job.
The writer was offered the job during the fair.
The writer dislikes the shop’s training program.
items.explanation: Watching videos and practicing on an old frame show effort made without being asked. The writer admitted never repairing a bike, so years of experience is false. The letter asks for an interview, so no offer exists yet, and the training is mentioned neutrally, with no sign of dislike. Strong inferences rest on actions the text actually reports.

items.stem:
Attendance at last year’s Redfern Career Fair reached nine hundred, up from six hundred the year before. Organizers credit two changes. First, a free shuttle now ran between the dormitories and the gymnasium every ten minutes. Second, the start time moved from eight in the morning to ten, which let students who work early shifts attend after finishing.

According to the brief, what did organizers say caused the rise in attendance?
options: A larger gymnasium and more printed resumes
Newspaper coverage and a lower admission fee
A free shuttle and a later start time
The addition of a second day of workshops
items.explanation: The passage names the shuttle and the later start as the two credited changes. A larger gymnasium, more resumes, newspaper coverage, a lower fee and a second workshop day are never mentioned, so each is an unsupported guess. In cause and effect items, look for signal words like credit, because and led to.

items.stem:
The Lindqvist Library volunteer tutoring program pairs adult helpers with students in grades three to six. Each pair meets twice a week for forty minutes, always at the same corner table. Volunteers receive a short training session on patient questioning, and they are asked to let students find answers rather than supply them. The coordinator says this habit builds confidence faster than correcting every mistake.

Why does the coordinator ask volunteers to let students find answers on their own?
options: It shortens each meeting to forty minutes.
It lets volunteers skip the required training session each month.
It keeps students from changing tables each week.
It builds confidence faster than correcting every mistake.
items.explanation: The last sentence gives the coordinator’s reason directly: the habit builds confidence faster. The forty minute length is a fixed schedule, training is required, and the corner table is simply the usual meeting place. Each wrong choice picks up a real detail but attaches it to the wrong cause.

items.stem:
Tutoring volunteers at Lindqvist Library choose from three weekly shifts. The table shows how many students signed up and how many volunteers are available for each.

Shift | Students | Volunteers
Monday evening | 18 | 12
Wednesday afternoon | 14 | 14
Saturday morning | 22 | 15

The coordinator wants every student paired with a volunteer. For which shift does the library most urgently need extra volunteers?
options: Monday evening
Saturday morning
Wednesday afternoon
All three shifts need the same number
items.explanation: Saturday morning is short by seven volunteers (22 students against 15 helpers), the largest gap. Monday evening is short by only six, Wednesday afternoon is already matched at fourteen each, and the gaps clearly differ. Subtracting volunteers from students in each row is the quickest comparison.

items.stem:
Parents of third graders received a flyer from the Lindqvist Library. It reads: “Is homework a nightly struggle? Our trained volunteers can help. Sessions are free, friendly and close to home. Sign up at the front desk today, because spaces fill quickly, and give your child a head start before the winter exams.”

What is the primary purpose of the flyer?
options: To persuade parents to enroll their children in tutoring
To describe the history of the library’s front desk
To report the results of last winter’s exams
To teach parents how to solve homework problems
items.explanation: The flyer opens with a worry, promises help, and ends with a call to sign up, which are persuasive moves. It never recounts the desk’s history, reports exam results, or teaches problem solving. Urgent phrases such as spaces fill quickly are a typical sign that the author wants action.

items.stem:
Text 1: Tutoring works best when sessions are frequent. A pair that meets twice a week remembers earlier lessons and spends less time reviewing.

Text 2: Frequency matters less than the match between helper and child. A pair that shares an interest, such as chess or birds, stays motivated even if it meets only once a week.

How do the two texts differ in their explanation of what makes tutoring succeed?
options: Text 1 stresses a shared interest, while Text 2 stresses how often pairs meet.
Both texts argue that chess and birds are the best tutoring subjects.
Text 1 stresses how often pairs meet, while Text 2 stresses a shared interest.
Text 1 opposes tutoring, while Text 2 supports it fully.
items.explanation: Text 1 credits twice a week meetings and less review, while Text 2 credits a shared interest even at one meeting weekly. Reversing the claims swaps the texts, the hobbies in Text 2 are only examples, and both texts support tutoring, so neither opposes it. Always label each claim with its own text.

items.stem:
When the Lindqvist program began, thirty children attended. Within a year the number had doubled, and a waiting list formed. The coordinator then recruited retired teachers, who each agreed to take on two extra pairs. As a result, the waiting list shrank to five names, and the corner table was joined by two more.

Which detail from the passage best supports the claim that recruiting retired teachers helped?
options: The waiting list shrank to five names afterward.
Thirty children attended when the program began.
The number of children doubled within a year.
The corner table was the usual meeting spot.
items.explanation: The shrinking waiting list is the outcome that follows the recruitment, so it is the evidence of help. The starting count and the doubling describe growth before the teachers arrived, and the table detail is background. Evidence must connect the cause, new teachers, to a result that came after it.

items.stem:
The city of Marlow Bay has launched a composting pilot in two neighborhoods. Households receive a green bin for food scraps, and trucks collect it every Friday. Scraps are carried to a yard on the east side, where they are mixed with leaves and turned weekly. After about ten weeks the mix becomes dark, crumbly soil that the parks department spreads on flower beds.

Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Marlow Bay trucks now collect all household waste every Friday.
Marlow Bay is testing a program that turns food scraps into soil for parks.
The parks department plans to replace its flower beds this year.
Leaves are the most valuable material in a compost yard.
items.explanation: The passage traces scraps from green bins to finished soil used in parks, so the pilot program is the central idea. Trucks collect only the green bins, flower bed replacement is never mentioned, and leaves are just one ingredient in the mix. Wrong choices inflate a minor detail into the whole point.

items.stem:
Compost yard crews at Marlow Bay track how quickly each batch breaks down. The table shows three batches that started on the same Monday.

Batch | Main ingredients | Weeks to finish
A | Food scraps and leaves | 10
B | Food scraps and sawdust | 13
C | Food scraps, leaves and grass | 8

According to the table, which statement is accurate?
options: Batch B finished sooner than Batch A, because it used sawdust.
Batch A contained grass clippings.
All three batches needed exactly ten weeks.
Batch C finished sooner than the other two batches.
items.explanation: Batch C needed eight weeks, fewer than the ten for A and thirteen for B. Batch B actually took longer than A, only Batch C lists grass, and the weeks differ across all three rows. Reading across each row, not down a single column, prevents mixing the batches up.

items.stem:
From the pilot report: Participation was stronger than expected. By week six, nearly nine of every ten households were setting out the green bin. However, crews found that many bins held plastic bags, which do not break down and must be picked out by hand. The department will therefore mail each household a simple card showing what may and may not go inside.

What is the relationship between the two parts of the passage joined by the word “However”?
options: The first part reports a success and the second introduces a problem.
The first part describes a problem and the second repeats it.
The first part gives a definition and the second gives an example.
Both parts list reasons for the pilot’s high participation.
items.explanation: The word however signals contrast: high participation is good news, while plastic bags in the bins are a difficulty. The report then states a fix. Nothing is defined, no example follows a definition, and the second part is not a reason for participation. Contrast words mark a turn in the structure.

items.stem:
Reviewer’s note: The kitchen pail that came with the pilot is better than I feared. It is small enough to fit beneath the sink, and the charcoal filter in its lid really does keep smells away, even in a warm week. My only complaint is the thin handle, which bends when the pail is full. A sturdier one would make it nearly perfect.

Which word best describes the reviewer’s overall tone?
options: Bitterly disappointed with the whole pail, from lid to handle
Completely neutral
Mostly approving, with one mild criticism
Confused and uncertain
items.explanation: The reviewer praises the size and the filter, then offers a single small complaint about the handle and calls the pail nearly perfect. That is approval with a mild criticism. Bitter disappointment overstates one flaw, neutrality ignores the praise, and nothing suggests confusion. Tone words should match how strongly the author expresses feeling.

items.stem:
Council members will vote next month on whether to expand the composting pilot citywide. Supporters point out that food scraps in landfills create waste that could become soil. Critics worry that weekly pickups will raise costs. The budget office has promised a full cost report before the vote, so that both sides can argue from the same numbers.

What can be inferred about the budget office’s purpose in preparing the cost report?
options: It hopes to block the vote altogether.
It wants the debate to rest on shared facts.
It favors the critics’ position over the supporters’.
It believes the pilot should end next month.
items.explanation: The report is promised so both sides can argue from the same numbers, which suggests a goal of factual, shared debate. Blocking the vote, favoring the critics, or ending the pilot would each require evidence of bias that the passage never gives. Inferences should follow from the stated reason, not from assumptions about hidden motives.

items.stem:
In 1931 Tram Number 14 carried commuters across Ostrava Heights, and for decades it rattled along the harbor line. Retired in 1968, it sat in a field until a volunteer group bought it for the price of scrap. Members have since replaced rotted floorboards, rewired the lamps, and repainted the cream and green stripes from an old photograph. They hope it will carry passengers again by autumn.

What is the author’s main purpose in this passage?
options: To persuade readers to ride trams instead of driving
To explain the electrical wiring of a vintage lamp
To compare the harbor line with other routes
To tell the story of a tram’s long journey back into service
items.explanation: The passage follows the tram from its working years through retirement to the restoration, so it tells a story. It never urges readers to ride, wiring is mentioned only once as a task, and no other routes are compared. Purpose questions are answered by what most of the passage actually does.

items.stem:
Restoring a tram takes patience. The volunteers first photographed every part before taking anything apart, so that each bolt could return to its place. Next they sorted pieces into labeled crates. Only then did they begin repairs, working from the frame upward. Ines Bartok, the project leader, says this order prevents mistakes that would cost weeks to undo.

Which sequence matches the order of the restoration steps described?
options: Photograph the parts, sort them into crates, then begin repairs.
Sort the parts into crates, begin repairs, then photograph the parts.
Begin repairs, photograph the parts, then sort them into crates.
Photograph the parts, begin repairs, then sort them into crates.
items.explanation: The passage uses first, next and only then to mark the sequence: photographs, crates, repairs. Each wrong order moves repairs ahead of the sorting or the photographs, which would defeat the leader’s goal of avoiding costly mistakes. Signal words such as first and next make the order easy to confirm.

items.stem:
Volunteer work shifts for the tram restoration are shown below. Each shift is led by one experienced member.

Day | Hours | Task
Tuesday | 6 to 9 p.m. | Wiring
Thursday | 6 to 9 p.m. | Painting
Saturday | 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. | Woodwork

A volunteer who works during the day and can only come on weekends should join which task?
options: Wiring
Painting
Wiring and painting together
Woodwork
items.explanation: Saturday is the only weekend shift, and its task is woodwork. Wiring is on Tuesday and painting on Thursday, both weekdays, so they do not fit a weekend only schedule. The table links each day to one task, and matching the volunteer’s limit to the day column gives the answer.

items.stem:
Text 1: The restored tram should be kept in a climate controlled museum, where its paint and wood will last for generations.

Text 2: A tram is built to move. Letting it carry passengers along the harbor line, even though weather will wear it, keeps its purpose alive for the people who come to see it.

On what point would the authors of the two texts most likely disagree?
options: Whether the tram was built in 1931
Whether restoration volunteers deserve thanks
Whether the tram should be preserved indoors or kept in use
Whether the harbor line still exists and carries any other trams
items.explanation: Text 1 wants the tram sheltered to last longest, while Text 2 wants it running even at the cost of wear. That is the clash. Neither text discusses the build date, the volunteers, or whether the harbor line exists. Disagreement lives in the claims each author actually makes.

items.stem:
Visitors often ask why the restored tram’s whistle sounds so thin. Engineer Paulo Reyes explains that the original brass bell and horn were sold years ago, so the team built a replacement from a drawing. It is accurate in shape but lighter in tone. A search for a surviving original continues, though Reyes admits the odds are slim.

What does the word “slim” most nearly mean in the passage?
options: gracefully narrow
very small
dull and quiet
recently measured
items.explanation: Odds that are slim means chances that are very small, and the sentence says the search may fail. Narrow in a graceful sense describes a shape, not a chance, dull and quiet confuses the odds with the thin sound, and recently measured has no link to the sentence. Context points to the meaning, not the usual physical sense.

items.stem:
Students at Kestrel Middle School were asked to rate the cafeteria lunches on a scale from one to five. The survey, answered by two hundred and forty students, showed that the vegetable soup earned the highest rating, while the cold sandwiches earned the lowest. Many students wrote that sandwiches arrived soggy because they were packed too early. The kitchen manager has promised to assemble them closer to serving time.

Why did students rate the cold sandwiches lowest?
options: Many found them soggy from being packed too early.
They were priced higher than the vegetable soup at every meal.
The kitchen manager refused to change them.
Few students answered questions about them.
items.explanation: Students wrote that the sandwiches arrived soggy because they were packed too early, which explains the low rating. Price is never discussed, the manager has promised a change, and two hundred and forty students answered the survey in general. Always look for the reason the passage itself gives.

items.stem:
The Kestrel lunch survey also asked how often students buy lunch instead of bringing it from home. Results are in the table.

Grade | Buy lunch daily | Bring lunch daily
Sixth | 60 | 20
Seventh | 45 | 35
Eighth | 30 | 50

Which conclusion do the results best support?
options: Sixth graders bring lunch more than eighth graders.
Seventh graders buy lunch more than sixth graders.
Eighth graders prefer soup to sandwiches.
The older the grade, the fewer students buy lunch daily.
items.explanation: Daily purchases fall from sixty to forty five to thirty as grades rise, so older students buy less. Sixth graders bring only twenty lunches against fifty for eighth graders, seventh graders buy fewer than sixth graders, and the table says nothing about soup preferences. Each wrong choice reverses or invents a trend.

items.stem:
Dear Parents: Thanks to your replies, we now know that many students skip breakfast and feel hungry by midmorning. Beginning Monday, the cafeteria will open twenty minutes before the first bell and sell fruit, yogurt and whole grain muffins at low cost. Students may pay with their regular lunch accounts. We hope the extra option makes mornings easier for your family.

What is the main purpose of this letter?
options: To collect overdue payments from parents for lunch accounts at once
To announce a new morning food service and explain why it exists
To ask parents to bake muffins for students
To report that the school survey has ended
items.explanation: The letter explains the finding about skipped breakfasts and announces a new service starting Monday. Payments are mentioned only as a convenience, parents are not asked to bake, and the survey is referred to only as the source of the finding. Purpose is what the whole letter does, not a single detail.

items.stem:
The student council member who presented the lunch survey spoke for only four minutes, yet the audience listened closely. She skipped long charts and offered three plain facts, each with a short story from a classmate. Afterward the principal remarked that she had made numbers feel like people.

Which inference about the presentation is best supported?
options: The audience was bored by the short length of the talk and left early.
The principal disliked the use of charts.
Pairing facts with personal stories made the data memorable.
The council member read every number aloud.
items.explanation: The audience listened closely and the principal said the numbers felt like people, so personal stories made the data memorable. Boredom contradicts the close listening, the principal never criticized charts, and she skipped long charts instead of reading numbers aloud. Inferences must agree with every detail given.

items.stem:
Text 1: The survey proves students want more choices. Only half of those polled were satisfied with the main dish, so the cafeteria should add a second one daily.

Text 2: Half satisfied does not mean half want a change. Some students may be content with what they have. The school should ask directly whether students want a second main dish.

How does Text 2 respond to Text 1?
options: It agrees that a second dish is needed immediately.
It questions whether the survey result supports the conclusion.
It argues that the survey was never conducted.
It proposes eliminating the main dish entirely and ending the survey.
items.explanation: Text 2 points out that dissatisfaction is not the same as wanting a change, challenging the link between the data and the conclusion. It does not agree with the plan, deny the survey happened, or propose removing the dish. A response to another text is identified by how it treats the first claim.

items.stem:
Researchers at the Garnet Point field station spent three summers measuring how fast the cliffs along Tern Bay are wearing away. They planted marker poles every fifty paces and recorded the distance from each pole to the cliff edge after every storm season. The poles nearest the open sea moved the most. The team concludes that waves, not rain, do most of the damage.

What did the researchers conclude from their measurements?
options: Rain erodes the cliffs faster than any other force along the shore.
Marker poles near the open sea were removed by visitors each summer.
The cliff edge stays at the same distance from every pole.
Waves cause most of the cliff damage.
items.explanation: Poles closest to the open sea showed the most movement, so the team blames waves. The text never credits rain, never says visitors removed poles, and reports distances that changed after storms, not a fixed distance. Conclusions should match the evidence the researchers actually gathered.

items.stem:
The Tern Bay study compares the cliff retreat recorded at three sections of shoreline over the same three summers.

Section | Faces | Average retreat in meters
North cove | Sheltered inlet | 2
Middle shore | Open sea | 9
South point | Open sea | 7

Which statement is best supported by the table?
options: The sheltered inlet lost more cliff than any other section.
South point retreated further than the middle shore.
Sections facing the open sea lost more cliff than the sheltered section.
All three sections lost nearly the same distance.
items.explanation: The two open sea sections lost nine and seven meters, far above the two meters at the sheltered cove. The cove did not lose the most, south point retreated less than the middle shore, and the totals are far from equal. Comparing the numbers in the last column row by row confirms the pattern.

items.stem:
Because the cliffs are made of soft sandstone, each storm tears away a layer about the thickness of a coin. Water then seeps into new cracks and freezes in winter, widening them until large blocks fall. A single cold week can undo what months of calm weather left intact. Homeowners near the edge have started moving back their fences.

According to the passage, what happens after water seeps into the cracks?
options: It freezes in winter and widens them until blocks fall.
It dissolves the sandstone into fine sand that drifts out to sea each day.
It hardens the cliff and slows the damage from storms.
It forces homeowners to sell their land.
items.explanation: The passage states that water in cracks freezes in winter and widens them until large blocks fall. Dissolving sandstone, hardening the cliff and forcing sales are not stated; the homeowners only move fences. A sequence in a text, seep, freeze, widen, fall, links each step to the next as cause and effect.

items.stem:
Dr. Ilse Moravec has studied the shoreline for twenty years. She walks the beach at dawn, long before the visitors arrive, notebook in hand. When asked about her findings she never exaggerates; she gives the number, the date and the doubts. A colleague jokes that she would hedge a sunrise. Even so, her reports are the ones the town council trusts most.

Which word best describes Dr. Moravec’s approach to her work?
options: Careless and hurried
Dramatic and boastful
Cautious and precise
Secretive and unhelpful
items.explanation: She reports numbers, dates and doubts and never exaggerates, so she is cautious and precise. Careless contradicts her careful notes, dramatic and boastful contradicts her refusal to exaggerate, and secretive contradicts reports the council trusts. The colleague’s joke about hedging a sunrise points to caution, not carelessness.

items.stem:
The town newsletter ran a short piece titled “Cliff Study Findings.” It opens with a fact about retreat rates, follows with a paragraph on the study methods, then lists three actions the council could take, and closes with a date for a public meeting. Readers said they understood what to do next.

Which description best fits the organization of the newsletter piece?
options: A story told in the order that the poles were planted
A finding, a method, a set of options and a next step
A list of definitions arranged in alphabetical order
A comparison of two competing theories about the sea
items.explanation: The piece moves from a finding to methods, then options, then a meeting date, so each part has a clear job. It is not told as a story of planting poles, it holds no alphabetized definitions, and it compares no theories. Naming the job of each paragraph reveals the structure.

items.stem:
From the keeper’s log, Saltmarsh Light: Fog rolled in at dusk and has not lifted. I lit the lamp at six and started the horn, which sounds every ninety seconds in thick weather. The oil level is good, and I polished the lens twice to keep it bright. One small fishing boat answered the horn near midnight, and I kept the light steady until it passed the rocks.

Which purpose is the keeper’s log entry most likely written to serve?
options: To record the night’s conditions and duties
To persuade fishermen to buy lamp oil
To advertise the lighthouse to tourists during the summer
To describe a dream the keeper once had
items.explanation: A log records what happened and what the keeper did, such as lighting the lamp, sounding the horn and guiding the boat. It makes no sales pitch, no tourist appeal and no dream account. The factual, time stamped details show the entry is a working record.

items.stem:
Saltmarsh Light, second night of fog. The horn failed at two o’clock because salt had crusted the valve. I cleaned it with a cloth and fresh oil, and it resumed at half past two. During the thirty minutes of silence I rang the hand bell every minute from the gallery. No vessel reported trouble, but I will check the valve each evening from now on.

What is the best explanation for the keeper’s decision to check the valve every evening?
options: The hand bell was louder than the horn and easier to reach.
No vessel reported trouble that night.
The oil level had fallen below the mark.
Crusted salt caused the horn to fail once already.
items.explanation: Salt crust on the valve stopped the horn, so daily checks aim to prevent a repeat. The bell was only a stopgap, the lack of vessel trouble shows luck, not a reason, and the oil is never said to be low. A plan makes sense when it answers the problem that came before it.

items.stem:
The keeper’s weekly supply schedule is shown below.

Day | Delivery | Time
Monday | Lamp oil | 8 a.m.
Wednesday | Groceries | 10 a.m.
Friday | Mail and newspapers | 2 p.m.

The supply boat can land only when the tide is high, and on Friday the keeper must be at the dock early to sign for any package. What can be concluded from the schedule?
options: The keeper’s mail arrives later in the day than the other deliveries.
Lamp oil and groceries are delivered on the same day.
The supply boat visits the lighthouse every day of the week.
Newspapers are delivered before the lamp oil each week.
items.explanation: Mail comes at 2 p.m., later than the 8 a.m. oil and 10 a.m. groceries. The oil and groceries come on different days, the boat visits only three days, and newspapers come Friday, after Monday’s oil. The Time column makes the comparison simple, so compare each hour in that column.

items.stem:
Text 1: A lighthouse keeper’s life is lonely. Months can pass with no conversation except the radio, and the lamp must be tended even when the keeper is ill.

Text 2: A lighthouse keeper’s life is rich with purpose. Every ship that passes safely is proof that the work mattered, and the sea provides a new view every morning.

Which statement best describes how the two texts treat the keeper’s life?
options: Both stress the dangers of fog and failing horns.
Text 1 praises the work and Text 2 complains about it.
Both describe the life, but Text 1 stresses hardship and Text 2 stresses meaning.
Neither text says anything about how the work feels.
items.explanation: Text 1 highlights loneliness and duty while ill, and Text 2 highlights purpose and daily views. Fog and horns are not mentioned in either, the texts do not swap praise and complaint, and both clearly speak about feelings. Compare what each text selects to emphasize.

items.stem:
When the automatic beacon replaced the keepers in 1984, many neighbors mourned. The tower, they felt, had lost its voice. Yet the beacon needed only a monthly visit, and the former keeper’s cottage became a small museum. Visitors today climb the stairs, ring the old hand bell and read the logs that proud keepers once wrote.

Which word best describes the author’s attitude toward the change?
options: Furious
Openly mocking
Fearful
Balanced
items.explanation: The author acknowledges the neighbors’ sadness, then notes the museum that grew from the change, giving both sides. Furious, mocking and fearful all assign a strong feeling that the passage never shows. A balanced tone presents loss and gain without leaning hard in one direction.

items.stem:
The Willowmere Tool Swap happens on the first Sunday of each month in the parking lot behind the hardware store. Neighbors bring tools they no longer use, such as hammers, ladders and garden shears, and trade them for items they need. Nothing is sold. A volunteer sharpens blades on the spot, and a table of safety gloves is free to everyone.

Which detail from the passage shows that money is not part of the swap?
options: A volunteer sharpens blades on the spot.
Nothing is sold.
The swap takes place on the first Sunday.
Neighbors bring hammers, ladders and shears.
items.explanation: The sentence stating that nothing is sold directly rules out money. The sharpening volunteer, the monthly date and the types of tools are all true but say nothing about payment. Supporting details must address the exact claim being tested, not merely appear in the same passage.

items.stem:
Organizer Tamsin Roy wrote in the newsletter: “A tool in a garage is a promise that nobody keeps. The drill that sat idle for five years can build three bookshelves in a neighbor’s home. That is why we trade rather than throw away.” She added that a ledger now lists who borrowed what.

What is the main reason Tamsin Roy gives for trading tools?
options: Neighbors enjoy building bookshelves every month.
A ledger now records everything that was borrowed.
Idle tools can be useful to someone else.
Hardware stores no longer sell drills.
items.explanation: Her example of a drill idle for five years that could build shelves elsewhere shows that unused tools are valuable to others. Enjoying shelf building is not her argument, the ledger is a rule she added later, and hardware stores are not described as stopping drill sales. A stated reason follows the word why.

items.stem:
Swap rules are posted on a sign at the entrance. Each person may bring up to five tools. Every tool must be clean and in working order. Power tools need a cord without cracks. Anyone who takes a tool must sign the ledger, and borrowed items return by the next swap day. Children under twelve must stay with an adult.

Which question can be answered using only the information in the sign?
options: How many neighbors attend each month?
Who built the parking lot?
What does a ladder usually cost?
How many tools may one person bring?
items.explanation: The sign states clearly that each person may bring up to five tools to the swap. Attendance numbers, who built the lot and the price of a ladder never appear. Questions that can be answered from the text have their answers in the text, so scan the sign for a number.

items.stem:
After the spring swap the volunteers counted what changed hands.

Item type | Brought | Taken
Hand tools | 40 | 36
Garden tools | 25 | 30
Power tools | 15 | 12

Garden tools were popular in spring. Which statement is best supported by the table?
options: More garden tools were taken than were brought.
More hand tools were taken than were brought.
More power tools were taken than were brought.
Garden tools were the largest group brought.
items.explanation: Garden tools show thirty taken against twenty five brought, so more left than arrived. Hand tools and power tools were taken in smaller numbers than brought, and hand tools, at forty, were the largest group brought. Compare each row’s two numbers separately, and never rely on the total alone to judge the trend.

items.stem:
Some neighbors worry that a tool swap invites broken equipment, so organizers added a repair corner. Two retired electricians test every power tool before it goes on the table, and a red tag marks anything unsafe. The result has been fewer complaints. Last year only one tool was reported faulty, and it was returned the same afternoon.

Which sentence best states the cause and effect relationship in the passage?
options: Fewer complaints led the organizers to add a repair corner.
The repair corner and red tags led to fewer complaints.
One faulty tool caused the electricians to retire.
Red tags were added because neighbors wanted more tools.
items.explanation: Organizers added testing and tags in response to worries, and the result was fewer complaints. Reversing the order, blaming retirement on a faulty tool, or tying tags to a wish for more tools all misread the sequence. Cause comes first, and the result follows, so check which event happened earlier in the passage.

items.stem:
After fourteen months of repairs, the Alder Street Bridge reopens to traffic on Monday at six in the morning. Crews replaced the worn deck, strengthened two support piers and added a separate lane for bicycles. Drivers should expect a lower speed limit while the new surface settles. A short ribbon ceremony will be held Sunday afternoon, and pedestrians may walk across before the cars return.

What is the best title for this news brief?
options: Alder Street Bridge Reopens After Major Repairs
Cyclists Demand Separate Lanes Across the City
Why Support Piers Wear Out Over Time
Ribbon Ceremony Cancelled by Heavy Rain
items.explanation: The brief reports the reopening and the repairs that came first, so that is the title that fits. The bike lane is only one repair, the piers are not the topic of an explanation, and the ceremony is scheduled, not cancelled. A good title covers the whole passage, not a single part.

items.stem:
Detour signs that guided drivers during the bridge repairs sent them eight blocks north along Pine Road. Shopkeepers on Alder Street say business dropped by about a third, because few drivers passed their doors. Now the owners are planning a sidewalk sale on the weekend of the reopening, hoping that the returning traffic will remember them.

Why are the shopkeepers planning a sidewalk sale?
options: They want to move to Pine Road permanently.
They plan to close their shops during the ribbon ceremony.
They hope returning traffic will bring back customers.
They are celebrating the end of the lower speed limit.
items.explanation: Business fell when detours sent cars north, so the sale aims to welcome traffic back. Moving to Pine Road, closing during the ceremony and celebrating a speed limit are not stated anywhere. Look for the purpose the passage names after the word hoping, since that phrase gives the shopkeepers’ goal.

items.stem:
An engineer’s inspection summary: The bridge deck now measures twelve inches thick, up from nine. The two strengthened piers show no cracks under a test load of heavy trucks. The bicycle lane is protected by a low barrier. One expansion joint on the north end is noisy, but it is safe, and crews will adjust it next month.

Which conclusion is supported by the summary?
options: The bridge must be closed again next month.
The bridge is safe to use even though one joint needs adjusting.
The piers failed the test with heavy trucks and must be replaced soon.
The bicycle lane has no barrier at all.
items.explanation: The report calls the noisy joint safe and says the piers showed no cracks under heavy trucks, so the bridge is safe. Closing it again, failed piers and the absence of a barrier all contradict the text. A conclusion cannot conflict with any stated fact.

items.stem:
Reopening day schedule:

Time | Event | Location
2 p.m. Sunday | Ribbon ceremony | North entrance
3 p.m. Sunday | Walking tour of the repairs | Center span
6 a.m. Monday | Traffic returns | Full bridge

A family wants to walk across the bridge and hear a talk about how it was repaired. Which event should they attend?
options: The ribbon ceremony on Sunday at 2 p.m.
Traffic returning on Monday at 6 a.m.
The ribbon ceremony and then traffic returning on Monday
The walking tour on Sunday at 3 p.m.
items.explanation: Only the walking tour is a walk across the bridge and covers the repairs. The ribbon ceremony is held at the entrance, and Monday morning is when cars, not pedestrians, return to the bridge. Match what the family wants with the event description and the place, not just the day of the week.

items.stem:
A letter signed by a resident reads: “For over a year my morning walk to the station meant a long detour and a missed train or two. I will not pretend I was patient. Still, when I stood on the new deck last week and watched the river slide below, the delay seemed a fair price for something this solid.”

Which word best describes the writer’s feelings at the end of the letter?
options: Grudgingly satisfied
Totally indifferent
Angry and bitter
Anxious about safety
items.explanation: The writer admits impatience but feels the delay was a fair price for a solid bridge, so satisfaction mixed with reluctance. Indifference ignores the effort to describe the view, anger and bitterness ignore the concession at the end, and safety fears conflict with solid. Tone often shifts after a word like still.

items.stem:
Each day at noon, a technician at the Brookfield weather station fills a rubber balloon with helium and lets it rise. Strapped beneath it is a lightweight sensor box that measures temperature, pressure and humidity. As the balloon climbs, it swells, because the air around it grows thinner. At about thirty kilometers it bursts, and the box drifts down on a small parachute.

How does the sensor box return safely to the ground?
options: It is lowered by a long cable from the station.
It drifts down on a small parachute.
It floats back as the helium cools.
It is caught by the technician in a net.
items.explanation: After the balloon bursts at about thirty kilometers, the box falls beneath a small parachute. No cable, cooling helium or net is mentioned. A how-it-works passage describes each step in order, so find the sentence that covers the final one and ignore the earlier steps.

items.stem:
The balloon swells as it climbs, and the passage gives a reason: the air around it grows thinner. With less air pressing from outside, the gas inside pushes the rubber outward until it can stretch no more.

What is the most likely effect of launching the balloon with too much helium?
options: It would never rise from the ground.
It would stop expanding as it climbs.
It would burst at a lower height than expected.
It would fall quickly with the sensor box.
items.explanation: Extra helium means the rubber is already stretched, so it reaches its limit sooner and bursts lower. The balloon would rise easily, not stay down, it would still expand as the air thins, and falling quickly would follow a burst, not extra gas. Reason from the stated cause of expansion.

items.stem:
Readings from one launch are shown in the table.

Height in kilometers | Temperature in degrees | Pressure level
0 | 15 | High
10 | minus 50 | Medium
20 | minus 55 | Low

According to the table, what happened to the pressure as the balloon climbed?
options: It rose from low to high.
It stayed at the same level.
It fell and then rose again.
It dropped from high to low.
items.explanation: The pressure column moves from high at the ground to medium and then low at twenty kilometers, a steady drop. Rising, staying level and falling then rising all contradict those three entries. Reading the column in order from top to bottom reveals the trend, so list the entries before choosing.

items.stem:
Students at Brookfield High will watch the next launch on Thursday. A teacher’s note says, “Bring warm clothes, a notebook and a pencil. We will stand in an open field, and the wind can be sharp even in spring. Each of you will record one reading, so please arrive ten minutes early to learn how.”

What is the primary purpose of the teacher’s note?
options: To prepare students for what to bring and do
To explain how helium differs from other gases
To warn students that the launch is canceled
To ask students to design a better balloon
items.explanation: The note lists clothing, supplies, the weather, a task and an arrival time, all of which prepare students. It does not discuss helium, the launch is going ahead, and no design work is requested. Notes of this kind aim to prepare the reader for an event.

items.stem:
Text 1: A launch like this one is the most reliable way to learn what the upper air is doing, because the sensor travels through it directly.

Text 2: Direct launches are useful but expensive and slow. Satellites scan the whole sky continuously, and the data arrive without anyone filling a single balloon.

What do the two texts have in common?
options: Both claim that balloons are cheaper than satellites.
Both say that satellites are unreliable.
Both agree that launches should end and satellites should replace them.
Both treat gathering information about the upper air as important.
items.explanation: Both texts concern ways to study the upper air, one praising launches and the other noting the value of satellites. Neither says balloons are cheaper, Text 2 praises satellites, and Text 2 calls launches useful, so neither wants them ended. Find the shared idea beneath the different opinions, since common ground is the point of the question.

items.stem:
The Thistledown rural clinic serves three villages and keeps a limited weekly schedule. Patients who need a visit outside those hours are asked to phone the nurse line.

Day | Hours | Service
Monday | 9 a.m. to noon | General checkups
Wednesday | 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. | Vaccinations
Friday | 9 a.m. to noon | Eye and hearing tests

A parent wants to bring a child for an immunization. Which visit should the parent plan?
options: Monday morning
Friday morning
Wednesday afternoon
Any weekday during opening hours
items.explanation: Vaccinations are offered only on Wednesday from one to four in the afternoon. Monday is for general checkups, Friday is for eye and hearing tests, and the clinic has no all week schedule. The parent should match the service column to the need, then confirm the day and hours listed beside it.

items.stem:
In the Alder Row bookbinding workshop, learners sew pages together in small bundles called signatures. They then press the bundles under weights for a full day, so the thread settles and the spine stays flat. Rushing this step, instructor Hana Lindgren warns, leads to a book that gapes open on one side. Patience, she says, is the cheapest tool in the room.

Why does Hana Lindgren warn against rushing the pressing step?
options: The thread would be too expensive to replace.
The book may gape open on one side.
The weights could damage the signatures.
Learners would run out of time in class.
items.explanation: She says that rushing leads to a book that gapes open on one side. Thread cost, damage from the weights and class time are not given as reasons. Her remark about patience being the cheapest tool is a comment on the value of waiting, not on money.

items.stem:
An electric bus trial begins in Corvane next month. Two buses will run on the number nine route, charging overnight at the depot. Riders are invited to fill in a card about comfort and noise. The transit office will study battery range, repair costs and rider feedback for six months before deciding whether to buy more.

What will the transit office decide at the end of the six months?
options: Whether to change the number nine route
Whether to close the overnight depot
Whether to survey riders about fares
Whether to buy additional electric buses
items.explanation: The passage says the office will study range, costs and feedback before deciding whether to buy more buses. The route, depot and fares are not described as decisions. The final sentence of a trial announcement usually names what the trial is meant to settle, so read it closely.

items.stem:
Bus driver Paolo Reyes, who has driven the number nine route for eleven years, took the first turn behind the wheel of the electric bus. He reported that hills felt easier, and the cabin was strangely quiet, so he could hear passengers talking. He admitted missing the rumble of the old engine, then smiled and said he could get used to the silence.

What can be inferred about Paolo Reyes’s reaction to the electric bus?
options: He is angry that it replaced older buses.
He is cautiously pleased with it.
He is afraid to drive it on hills.
He has no opinion about it.
items.explanation: He praised the easier hills and quiet cabin, while admitting to missing the old rumble, so his view is cautiously positive. Anger, fear on hills and having no opinion all contradict his remarks. Mixed feelings that lean to the positive point to cautious approval, and the details support that reading.

items.stem:
Text 1: Electric buses cost more to buy, but their fuel and repairs cost less each year, so the savings can recover the price within a decade.

Text 2: Electric buses cost more to buy, and batteries must be replaced about halfway through a bus’s life. The savings may shrink, and no one knows yet how large they will be.

How do the two texts differ?
options: Text 1 says buses cost less to buy, and Text 2 says they cost more.
Text 1 ignores fuel costs, and Text 2 ignores batteries.
Text 1 expects savings to recover the cost, and Text 2 is uncertain.
Text 2 praises the buses, and Text 1 rejects them.
items.explanation: Both agree on the higher purchase price, but Text 1 expects the savings to repay it while Text 2 raises battery replacement and uncertainty. Each wrong choice misstates one text. Neither says the price is lower, Text 1 does discuss fuel costs, and neither praises or rejects the buses outright.
